title: Endoscopic Buccal Mucosal Grafting of the Glottis
source_label: Operative Techniques in Laryngology (Rosen and Simpson, eds, 2024), Ch 29 Buccal Mucosal Grafting in the Larynx
indications: Full-thickness buccal mucosa can resurface membranous vocal fold mucosal defects larger than about 5 mm after resection of carcinoma, papilloma, or scar, to prevent or treat an anterior glottic web, or as primary reconstruction after selected T1a cordectomy. Thin grafts replace mucosa only; thicker grafts add bulk after vocalis resection. The graft is held against the recipient bed with a Silastic-backed transcervical suture bolster for about 2 weeks. Adequate transoral exposure of the full fold is required. Contraindications include cartilaginous anterior stenosis, uncertain cancer margins (the graft hides the surveillance site), and T1b disease, and prior radiation or poor healing raises the risk of graft failure.
setup: Confirm exposure in clinic or at prior laryngoscopy; poor exposure is a contraindication.
After cancer resection, frozen-section margins must be clear before grafting.
Suspension microlaryngoscopy set, microscope, cup forceps, and microinstruments.
Oral harvest tray: cheek retractor, 15 blade, lidocaine with epinephrine, fine suture.
Reinforced 0.4 mm Silastic sheeting, 5-0 chromic, 2-0 polypropylene, 19 to 20 gauge hollow needles (or Lichtenberger needle carrier).
danger: Injury to the parotid duct at harvest
Harvest too close to the oral commissure
Needle passage too high or low relative to the fold
steps: Confirm the indication

Use for membranous vocal fold mucosal defects larger than about 5 mm after resection of cancer, papilloma, or scar, to prevent or treat an anterior web, or as primary reconstruction after selected T1a resection. Confirm adequate transoral exposure, since the graft and needles must be placed under direct vision.
Prepare the recipient bed

Create a clean raw surface on the membranous fold under suspension microlaryngoscopy and confirm clear frozen margins after cancer resection. When both folds are raw, graft only one side, since the other heals secondarily, and do not span the anterior commissure, which blunts it. Achieve hemostasis so no hematoma lifts the graft.
Measure the defect

Measure the defect; most grafts are about 1 x 1 cm. Thin grafts of 0.5 to 1 mm replace mucosa only, while thicker grafts of about 2 mm add bulk after vocalis resection. Plan the harvest size accordingly.
Harvest buccal mucosa

Remove the laryngoscope, evert the cheek, and infiltrate lidocaine with epinephrine. Harvest a full-thickness graft with a 15 blade below the parotid duct papilla and at least 1.5 cm behind the oral commissure, without going deep to buccinator. Trim fat from the deep surface and close the donor site with chromic.
Mount the graft

Cut a 1.5 x 1.5 cm square of 0.4 mm reinforced Silastic and lay the graft mucosal side against it with the raw side facing up. Tack the corners with 5-0 chromic so the graft and sheet move as one unit.
Place the holding suture

Pass a 2-0 polypropylene suture through the graft and sheet and back, leaving both long ends on the raw side. These ends will be pulled out through the neck to draw the construct firmly onto the recipient bed.
Reinsert the laryngoscope
Replace and suspend the laryngoscope and clear blood and debris from the defect under the microscope. Confirm the recipient bed is still dry and the full defect is visible before passing needles.
Pass transcervical needles

Insert one 19 to 20 gauge needle through the thyroid cartilage or cricothyroid membrane below the fold, and a second through the thyroid cartilage into the ventricle above the mid-membranous fold, angled slightly upward. Flush both needles to clear cartilage debris from the lumen.
Thread the suture

Using cup forceps under magnification, thread each polypropylene end through a hollow needle and out to the neck; a Lichtenberger needle carrier is an alternative. Withdraw the needles, leaving the suture ends exiting the skin.
Seat the graft
Pull the sutures to draw the Silastic-backed graft into the larynx and against the defect, then confirm with telescopes that the graft covers the raw area and sits at the free edge without folding.
Tie externally

Thread both suture ends through a second Silastic square on the neck skin and tie with enough tension to immobilize the sandwich of Silastic, graft, fold, cartilage, and skin. Too little tension allows shear; too much causes skin necrosis.
Extubate carefully

Extubate gently, avoiding bucking that could shear the graft, and observe the airway, discharging once breathing is stable. Start reflux therapy and advise avoiding forceful coughing and throat clearing during the healing period.
Second stage at 2 weeks
Under brief anesthesia, cut the external suture, divide the chromic tacks, and peel the Silastic off the graft gently so the graft is not dislodged. Inspect for take and trim any redundant edges.
Follow-up

Expect graft swelling and limited voice at 1 week, followed by revascularization and gradual gains in pliability over the next month. Follow with stroboscopy and voice therapy as needed to optimize closure and vibration.
exit_check: Graft seated flat against the defect on angled telescope
External bolster tied with appropriate tension
Donor site hemostatic and parotid duct intact
postop: Reflux therapy and avoid forceful cough or throat clearing
Stroboscopy and voice therapy over the following months

early: Neck skin pressure injury from bolster

attending_followup: Why use buccal mucosa for vocal fold resurfacing?
It is readily available, thin and pliable, epithelialized with a lamina propria that can revascularize, and leaves a well-tolerated donor site.
What structures limit the buccal harvest site?
The parotid duct papilla superiorly and the oral commissure anteriorly (stay at least 1.5 cm behind it).
When is a thicker graft chosen?
After vocalis resection, when bulk is needed in addition to mucosal coverage.
What keeps the graft in place during healing?
A Silastic sandwich held by transcervical polypropylene sutures tied over a second Silastic square on the neck.
At about 2 weeks under brief anesthesia, peeling the Silastic off without dislodging the graft.
source_basis: Rosen CA, Simpson CB. Operative Techniques in Laryngology, 2nd ed (2024), Chapter 29 (Woo P): Buccal Mucosal Grafting in the Larynx (pp 239-244)
